title: GPU power-shedding and handoff playbook for latency-sensitive inference
body:
Purpose and scope
This playbook describes an operational design for graceful GPU power-shedding and request handoff across heterogeneous inference fleets (A100, H100, L4, MI300). It focuses on latency-sensitive model serving (chat/generation, short-sequence retrieval rerankers) where transient power/thermal headroom constraints must not cause large SLO violations. The goal is to: (1) maintain P99 latency SLOs where possible, (2) avoid hard OOM/thermal kills, and (3) degrade output quality predictably via quantized/shortened kernels or routing to cheaper model variants.

Audience
- Serving runtime engineers implementing schedulers and kernel selection
- SRE/ops for GPU fleet configuration and alerting
- Solutions engineers who map customer latency requirements to deployment profiles

High-level approach
1) Observability-first: detect impending power/thermal pressure early using moving-window metrics (5–30s) and per-GPU trends rather than instant spikes.
2) Tiered degradation: escalate through controlled mitigations with bounded user-visible impact: reduce per-request throughput (deferred batching), switch to quantized/fast-kernel, partially evict/trim KV cache, and finally handoff to alternate device class or region.
3) Fast handoff: provide a warm-path migration for requests that can't be satisfied within latency SLO on the originating GPU. Handoff must preserve request context, minimal token loss, and respect privacy/tenant isolation.

Signals and thresholds (recommendation)
- NVML power draw (W): primary signal for power cap triggers; set soft threshold at 90% of configured power_cap averaged over 15s, hard threshold at 98% averaged over 5s.
- GPU temperature (°C): warn at 75°C sustained (30s), escalate at 85°C.
- SM utilization (%): sustained >85% plus high queue depth => consider KV/memory pressure.
- PCIe/Host-to-device bandwidth saturation: >85% and rising => prefer smaller kernels / compressed payloads.
- Request queue latency (ms): if P50 queue latency > 30ms for latency-sensitive routes, trigger pre-emptive batching or kernel fallback.
- KV cache hit rate: a drop >10 percentage points correlated with increased memory churn suggests aggressive KV eviction may be harmful.

Degradation ladder (actions, ordered low-to-high impact)
1) Dynamic kernel parameter adjustment (lowest impact)
   - Switch to lower-latency kernel variants (fused attention, reduced tiling) for short seq lengths.
   - Adjust per-model kernel priority so smaller/interactive models preempt large-batch kernels.
   - Per-GPU knob: kernel_throttle_pct (reduce kernel concurrency by 10–30%).
2) Intra-GPU request shaping
   - Reduce max_batch_size by 1 step for affected models (configurable hierarchy).
   - Enforce strict preemptive scheduling for p99-critical routes (give them KV-prewarmed lanes).
3) KV cache micro-eviction (soft)
   - Identify least-recently-used prefix shards where rewarm cost < threshold (measured by token re-gen CPU cost).
   - Evict selectively by prefix length (prefer pruning deeper history first so immediate context is preserved).
   - Metrics: measure rewarm miss tail latency impact in canary lanes before global rollout.
4) Quantization/precision fallback (predictable quality drop)
   - Fall back from fp16 to int8-quantized kernels (or 4-bit) for non-critical shards when power headroom insufficient.
   - Use config profiles per-model: quality_budget (max acceptable ROUGE/EM drop) to decide quantization.
5) Cross-GPU handoff (highest complexity)
   - Route new requests to a sibling GPU in same host with spare headroom, then to different host in same rack, then cross-rack.
   - Handoff must transfer minimal KV context: send KV prefix checksum + on-demand fetch of hot slices.
   - Use warm pool of lightweight replicas (small quantized copies) for emergency handoff to minimize warmup.

Per-hardware considerations
- A100 (sustained throughput workhorse)
  - Typical power_cap: 250–300W. Soft threshold: 225W.
  - Behavior: good sustained throughput but sensitive to sustained high SM utilization causing PCIe stalls.
  - Recommended mitigations: prioritize kernel coalescing, keep KV slices local, avoid large on-GPU batch consolidation when thermal headroom low.
- H100 (high peak perf, thermal spikes)
  - Typical power_cap: 300–350W. Soft threshold: 315W.
  - Behavior: more aggressive turbo -> faster temperature ramp. Use shorter sampling windows for temperature signals (5–10s).
  - Recommended mitigations: early quantization fallback, shorter kernels, aggressive per-request pacing.
- L4 (edge/efficient)
  - Typical power_cap: 75–125W. Soft threshold: 90% nominal.
  - Behavior: limited KV capacity, limited multi-request concurrency.
  - Recommended mitigations: conservative batching, route large-seq requests away; prefer compressed payloads.
- MI300 (large memory & chiplet topology)
  - Typical power_cap: 400–500W. Soft threshold: 0.9*cap.
  - Behavior: excellent large-model memory headroom but NUMA-like local memory effects. Watch inter-chiplet bandwidth saturation.
  - Recommended mitigations: prefer KV sharding aligned to chiplet affinity, avoid cross-chiplet handoffs for hot KV slices.

Kernel selection rules (runtime mapping)
- Maintain a small matrix for each model: {seq_length_buckets, batch_buckets} -> preferred kernel variant + expected power profile. Keep this matrix as a first-class artifact and feed it to the scheduler.
- Example: seq<=64 & batch<=4 -> low-latency fused attention kernel (power moderate); seq>512 -> tiled kernel optimized for throughput (power high).

KV cache policies to support handoff
- Make hot-slice replication configurable: N_hot_replicas per model. Increase N for low-latency routes at cost of memory.
- Store KV metadata (prefix checksums, last-access time, approximate size) in a fast host-index to allow quick decision if handoff needs context.
- During handoff, prefer on-demand fetch of only the top-k most recent KV slices rather than whole prefix transfer.

Operational playbook (SRE runbook steps)
1) Alert: 90% power threshold sustained -> set swarm flag power_shedding_active=true and apply kernel_throttle_pct=15 on affected hosts. Notify on-call.
2) If temperature escalation -> escalate to quantization fallback profile for non-critical routes and increase KV_preservation=false for batch lanes.
3) If P99 latency SLO breaches persist after 60s -> trigger cross-GPU handoff for new incoming requests and drain non-critical long-running requests off the host.
4) Post-incident: collect NVML traces, kernel timelines, KV eviction logs, and run automated regression on a replay cluster to tune thresholds.

Experimentation and validation plan
- Synthetic microbench: bursty short-sequence workload (token/s bursts) with controlled power caps to validate ladder sequence and measure SLO vs. quality tradeoffs.
- Canary: enable playbook in a small subset (2–5%) of traffic for 72h with full observability.
- Metrics to track: P50/P95/P99 latency, request success rate, KV hit-rate, quality regressions (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-sim as applicable), power cap events, handoff count and handoff-induced tail latency.

Open questions / next steps
- Should handoff include partial speculative prewarm on sibling GPUs to reduce transfer latency? (experiments needed)
- Tradeoff curve between KV replication factor and memory overhead needs per-model profiling automation.
- Integration with existing rollout/traffic-split logic (console) for safe canarying.

Appendix: quick knobs and defaults (starting point)
- kernel_throttle_pct: 15
- power_soft_pct: 0.90
- power_hard_pct: 0.98
- temp_warn_c: 75
- temp_escalate_c: 85
- max_kv_eviction_pct_per_min: 5
- handoff_prefer_same_host: true

Action items
- [ ] Implement power_shedding flag and kernel_throttle_pct in serving runtime (Evan)
- [ ] Add NVML-based rolling-window power alarm to node exporter (Sofia)
- [ ] Create canary config and run synthetic burst tests (Priya & Jamal)

Notes: this is intended as a working playbook draft. Keep experimental config values conservative and prefer observability before automated aggressive mitigations.
